lesson: Before capturing a piece, check if it's defended or if the capture allows a recapture that wins material back.
When pushing a passed pawn vs grabbing material, calculate whether advancing the pawn immediately wins faster than detours.
In rook endgames, prefer active/checking rook moves (e.g., checks, cutting off king) over passive trades that let the opponent's king activate.
In king-and-pawn endgames, verify the exact king opposition/distance before pushing a passed pawn; sometimes a king move secures the win faster.
Before a central pawn capture, check if it opens lines or hangs pieces to tactics like knight forks or discovered attacks.
When repositioning a piece, check if it abandons a key defended square or hangs the queen/piece to an immediate tactic.
In king-and-pawn endgames, calculate the key squares precisely—don't rely on general "opposition" intuition when a pawn is nearby.
Before moving a knight to a square attacked by enemy pawns or pieces, confirm it isn't simply captured for free next move.
When your king endgame is drawn or winning, double-check candidate king moves against the specific key-square rule rather than assuming any safe-looking move works.
Before trading queens or simplifying for a "clean" material gain, scan for alternative moves (like Bg5) that win more material or keep attack alive.
When ahead in rook endgames, prioritize keeping rooks active and opponent's king cut off rather than trading rooks to "simplify" when material is already behind.
After each candidate move, explicitly list all enemy pieces attacking the destination square before committing to the capture or trade.
When a knight is attacked, verify the retreat square isn't itself attacked by a pawn advance (like d5) before moving there.
Before committing a knight to a seemingly strong outpost, calculate opponent's immediate pawn pushes that could trap or win it.
When choosing between two retreat squares, prefer the one furthest from enemy pawn advances, not just the "safe-looking" one.
Before capturing or trading, check if the opponent has an undefended piece hanging via a stronger move like a bishop fork/capture on a back-rank square.
After opponent offers a trade (like Qxd8), check if declining to capture their piece first wins material instead of recapturing passively.
When material grab looks "free," scan all opponent pieces eyeing the capturing square first, including bishops and knights, not just pawns.
When a piece is attacked, check all legal capturing moves (not just recaptures) before retreating, since a counter-capture may win material outright.
Before giving an "attacking" check or queen move, verify the target square isn't also guarded by another enemy piece causing a losing exchange.
When your queen or piece dives deep into enemy territory, check all retreat squares are covered, or you risk being trapped and mated.
In king-and-pawn endgames with a winning position, avoid repeating king moves aimlessly; calculate a concrete plan to make progress.
Before capturing a pawn with check, check if the destination square is defended by another piece that recaptures favorably.
When already winning comfortably, prioritize the simplest safe plan over tactical shots that risk squandering the advantage.
In king-and-pawn endgames with a near-queening pawn, check if your own king's advance blocks the pawn or creates stalemate risk.
In won endgames, verify that pushing your pawn or advancing your king doesn't remove your opponent's only legal moves, causing stalemate.
In symmetrical pawn structures, calculate concrete piece trades (e.g., dxe4) rather than mirroring opponent's central pawn pushes by default.
